title: The hero Nikole Hannah-Jones could have been
author: Alexander Russo
summary: Education journalism critic Alexander Russo, who has written about Nikole Hannah-Jones more than ten times, responds to her latest New York Times piece by arguing that her pattern of reversals has repeatedly cost vulnerable students a powerful advocate. He traces three moments. First, her deeply reported case that segregation was the core problem in schooling and integration its solution, which he says she abandoned when choosing a school for her daughter without fully acknowledging the shift. Second, a weekend in May 2020 when she criticized the lack of live instruction for vulnerable children during school closures, then apologized for the appearance of teacher bashing and withdrew from the debate within 72 hours. Third, her new piece, in which he says she has again reversed herself by choosing a screened school while downplaying the caring, learning-focused schools that serve all kinds of children. His complaint is less about inconsistency than about missed moments when her platform could have changed minds and prompted action for the children she has championed.
points: Russo credits Hannah-Jones with building herself into a national conscience on educational inequity before faulting her follow-through.
He singles out the 2020 remote learning debate as her best chance to help break the impasse that kept blue-city schools closed.
He argues her latest piece overlooks schools that successfully serve all kinds of students, the very examples her readers need.
The critique is framed around unrealized advocacy for vulnerable kids rather than simple charges of hypocrisy.
quotes: My beef — as an education journalist and as an admirer of her work — is not so much that she’s reversed herself (repeatedly) but rather that she’s missed the chance to stand up for the vulnerable kids she’s so often said she’s championing
Over the past decade, Hannah-Jones used her prodigious talents and efforts to build herself into a national conscience on the inadequate education so many children receive.
First, she convinced most of us with deeply reported stories that school segregation was the core problem we should all be writing about — and that integration was the obvious solution.
However, the debate about schools being shut down without virtual instruction was Hannah-Jones’ chance to be a real hero

There was no one I can imagine better positioned to change minds and prompt action. But Hannah-Jones abandoned the effort no more than 72 hours into the fight, and subsequently did little writing on the topic.
Given a chance to focus attention on the inadequacies of too many schools — and the possibilities shown by many others — she’s instead reversed herself yet again
